summary: The manuscript compares a random-matrix-theory forecaster (RPM) with learning-curve extrapolation and simple rules on 38 public calibration tasks. The design is pre-registered, uses paired comparisons on identical pilots, and provides per-pilot raw outputs, so most of the inference can be re-checked. One headline result holds up under every re-analysis I ran: RPM is more accurate and less optimistic than IPL3. It is better in 9/9 data sources and 11/11 spectral libraries, and source-level Wilcoxon p = 0.004. Most other inferential claims are weaker than presented. Several are wrong. (i) The 38 tasks are not independent units. ICRAF-MIR and ICRAF-VisNIR share all 4,153 soil samples and their reference values, and the properties within each library share spectra. (ii) 'SLOPE-T significantly better than RPM' and 'RPM-w significantly better than RPM' are post-hoc results with fragile multiplicity. They do not hold under the PLS truth or without the ICRAF-VisNIR tasks. The text nonetheless says the PLS ordering was unchanged and the sensitivity analysis changed no conclusion. (iii) Equivalence ('equally accurate', 'as accurate as any method') is claimed from non-significance. (iv) The pilot's minimum-CV error, which anchors FLAT, SLOPE-T, the gain analysis and the decision metric, is optimistically biased by 0.19/0.11/0.06 log units at n0 = 50/100/200. FLAT's accuracy therefore comes largely from two biases that cancel. (v) The post-hoc conformal bands reach nominal coverage only when pooled. Conditional coverage is 64% at n0 = 25 and 29–50% for CGL, Tablets and Diesel. (vi) The transferred slope (8.3% per doubling) is in effect a soil-library constant that depends on the n-range. With leave-one-family-out transfer, SLOPE-T is worse than RPM on 29/38 tasks. Ground-truth Monte-Carlo and test-set error are not reported. My perturbation analysis shows they do not overturn the task-level tests, but they matter for the coverage evaluation.
strengths: Pre-registered primary endpoint, unit of analysis (task), test (two-sided Wilcoxon) and multiplicity rule. A time-stamped decision log separates pre-registered from post-hoc elements, and negative results (RPM-T, the decision metric, FLAT) are reported.

Fully paired design: every method is evaluated on the same pilots and horizons, and per-pilot raw forecasts are released. Every inferential statement can therefore be re-analysed. I recomputed Table 2/S8 statistics from raw_results.csv and they match.

The central confirmatory claim, that RPM is less optimistic and more accurate than IPL3, survives a cluster-level re-analysis. RPM is better in 9/9 sources and 11/11 libraries (source-level Wilcoxon p = 0.004; library-level p = 0.001), and the cluster-bootstrap 95% CI of the task-mean IPL3−RPM difference is [+0.089, +0.213]. It also holds against the PLS truth and without ICRAF-VisNIR.
Leave-one-source-out construction of the transferred priors (RPM-T, SLOPE-T) and of the conformal bands avoids direct target leakage.
Twenty pilots per task and pilot size is adequate for task-level means. The median pilot-sampling SE of the per-task FLAT−RPM difference is 0.018, against a between-task SD of 0.078 (my computation).

issues.title: The 38 tasks are not independent units; Wilcoxon tests and bootstrap CIs over tasks ignore clustering by library and source
issues.description: Section 3.7 treats the 38 tasks as independent paired observations. Both the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and the bootstrap over tasks assume this. In fact the tasks are nested: 4 properties per soil library share the same spectra, soils and pools, and 23/38 tasks come from one family (OSSL soils). Libraries also share physical samples across instruments: every ICRAF-MIR sample is also in ICRAF-VisNIR, with identical reference values, so ICRAF-MIR:OC and ICRAF-VisNIR:OC are the same soils and the same y. The effective number of independent units is therefore nearer the 9 sources (or 6 'sources' in the abstract) than 38. This inflates the significance of small effects, and the reported CIs are too narrow.
issues.evidence: Manuscript Section 3.7 ('The task is the unit of analysis'); Table 1. Sample overlap from code/data/cache: ossl_ICRAF_ISRIC_mir.npz ids 4,153, all of them in ossl_ICRAF_ISRIC_visnir.npz (overlap 4,153/4,153). KSSL MIR/VisNIR share 20,969 layer ids. My source-level re-analysis (per-task mean errors averaged within the 9 sources used by source_of() in analysis.py): RPM vs IPL3 holds (RPM better in 9/9 sources, Wilcoxon p = 0.004; 11/11 libraries, p = 0.001). RPM-w vs RPM does not (RPM-w better in only 5/9 sources, p = 0.65; cluster bootstrap of the task-mean difference −0.013, 95% CI [−0.026, +0.004]), although the manuscript reports it as significant (Holm p = 0.023). FLAT vs RPM: 7/9 sources, p = 0.13. Cluster-bootstrap CIs (resampling sources) of the mean task error are wider than the reported i.i.d. CIs: FLAT [0.204, 0.341] vs reported 0.227–0.315; IPL3 [0.353, 0.503] vs 0.375–0.496. Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R4/a2.py, a10.py.
issues.corrective_action: Keep the pre-registered task-level analysis but add a pre-declared clustered analysis: (a) a linear mixed model of per-task log errors with random effects for library within source (or a cluster-robust paired test); (b) source-level sign/Wilcoxon tests; (c) cluster bootstrap (resampling sources) for all CIs in Table 2 and S8. Report the effective number of independent units. State explicitly that ICRAF-MIR/VisNIR and KSSL-MIR/VisNIR tasks share samples and reference values. Restrict 'significant' to claims that survive clustering.

issues.title: Post-hoc 'significant' claims (SLOPE-T > RPM, RPM-w > RPM) rest on an inconsistent multiplicity scope and do not survive the paper's own sensitivity analyses; two statements about those analyses are false
issues.description: The pre-registration specifies Holm correction 'across baselines' (the 6 registered baselines). The analysis puts the 4 post-hoc methods (RPM-w, RPM-T, RPM-wT, SLOPE-T) into the same family as the 6 registered baselines. Because Holm is step-down, the many near-zero p-values of the registered comparisons make the post-hoc SLOPE-T comparison cheap to pass (multiplier 2). The same raw p (0.0155) receives Holm p = 0.031 in Table S8 and 0.046 in Table S9 (SLOPE-T as reference), which shows how arbitrary the family choice is. About 110 hypothesis tests are reported in at least 12 separately corrected families (S8, S9, S10, S13, S15, S23, S24, S17, S32–S35, plus uncorrected Spearman tests), with no statement of overall error control. The main text then claims that SLOPE-T was 'significantly better than the pre-registered RPM' and that RPM-w's difference to RPM 'was significant'. It also claims that 'against the PLS ground truth the ordering was unchanged' and that 'excluding the four ICRAF-VisNIR tasks ... changed no conclusion'. The numbers contradict both statements.
issues.evidence: statistics.json ridge: SLOPE-T vs RPM p_raw = 0.0155, p_holm = 0.031, bootstrap 95% CI of the median difference [−0.049, +0.0016], which includes 0. tables/T3c: same comparison, p_holm = 0.046. statistics.json pls: SLOPE-T vs RPM p_holm = 0.328. tables/S0_stats_excluding_ICRAF_VisNIR.csv: SLOPE-T vs RPM p_holm = 0.107; RPM-w vs RPM p_holm = 0.107. Ordering under ridge truth (Table 2): SLOPE-T 0.251 < FLAT 0.266 < RPM 0.284. Under PLS truth (Section 4.3 text, Table S12): FLAT 0.253 < SLOPE-T 0.263 < RPM 0.279, so the ordering did change. Under the PLS truth, FLAT vs RPM has p_raw = 0.027 and a CI excluding 0 [−0.053, −0.006], with FLAT better on 26/38 tasks. Source-level analysis for SLOPE-T vs RPM: p = 0.039 (ridge) but 0.129 (PLS). EXPERIMENT_LOG.md 14:53 marks SLOPE-T as 'not pre-registered'.
issues.corrective_action: (1) Restrict the confirmatory Holm family to the six pre-registered baselines vs RPM, as registered. (2) Treat all post-hoc comparisons as exploratory: report unadjusted p-values as descriptive, or apply one correction across all post-hoc tests in the paper, and avoid the word 'significant' for them. (3) Correct the false statements in Section 4.3: the PLS ordering changed (FLAT < SLOPE-T), and the ICRAF-VisNIR exclusion removes the significance of both RPM-w vs RPM and SLOPE-T vs RPM. (4) In the abstract and conclusions, present SLOPE-T's advantage over RPM as a hypothesis-generating observation.

issues.title: Equivalence is claimed from non-significance, and the failure of the pre-registered hypothesis against simple rules is understated
issues.description: The pre-registered RQ2 asks whether RPM forecasts 'more accurately than learning-curve extrapolation and simple rules', and hypothesis (b) predicts superiority. Against the registered simple rule FLAT, RPM was nominally worse (FLAT better on 23/38 tasks; median difference −0.021). The paper never states that this part of the pre-registered hypothesis was not supported. Instead it asserts equivalence: 'were equally accurate' (Abstract), 'as accurate as any method tested' (Recommendation ii), 'forecast future RMSE as well as any extrapolation' (Conclusions), 'no significant difference among the first three' (Section 4.3), 'changed no conclusion' (Section 4.3). No equivalence margin or equivalence test is specified. The CIs are compatible with practically relevant differences in both directions.
issues.evidence: statistics.json ridge FLAT vs RPM: median difference −0.021, 95% CI [−0.047, +0.010], Holm p = 0.148 (FLAT nominally better). PLS: CI [−0.053, −0.006], p_raw = 0.027 (FLAT better on 26/38). SLOPE-T vs FLAT (Table S9): p = 0.161, CI of median difference [−0.003, +0.042]. Ratio ≥ 16 stratum (Table S10): only comparisons against RPM-w were tested, so 'no significant difference among the first three' was never tested for SLOPE-T vs FLAT. Pre-registration (supplementary/EXPERIMENT_DESIGN_preregistration.md, Hypothesis (b) and RQ2).
issues.corrective_action: State explicitly in the abstract and conclusions that the pre-registered superiority of RPM over the simple no-improvement rule was not supported, and that FLAT was nominally better. Pre-specify and justify an equivalence margin (e.g. 0.05 log units ≈ 5% RMSE, related to the pilot-CV sampling error). Run TOST (paired, task- or cluster-level) for every claim of 'equal' or 'as accurate as'. Otherwise replace these phrases with 'not significantly different (95% CI ...)'.

issues.title: The pilot's minimum-CV error is optimistically biased. FLAT and SLOPE-T accuracy rests on cancelling biases, and the gain and decision analyses are distorted by the same anchor
issues.description: FLAT and SLOPE-T forecast from pilot_cv = min over the 53-point penalty grid of the LOGO-CV MSE (forecast_experiment.py: pilot_cv = np.min(f['path'])). The same anchor is used for the post-hoc gain analysis and is prepended to every method's curve in the decision metric (analysis.py decision_table, posthoc_gain). Compared with the ground truth at n = n0, this anchor is systematically too low. Two mechanisms are likely: selection optimism of the minimised CV, and the truth being log of an arithmetic-mean MSE over heavy-tailed repetitions. The manuscript's interpretation that FLAT's 'error equals the true improvement between n0 and n' (Section 4.3) is therefore wrong. FLAT's error is anchor bias plus improvement, and the two partly cancel. Without the anchor bias, FLAT would be clearly worse than RPM. SLOPE-T's optimism (bias −0.093) is almost entirely anchor bias. In the gain analysis, RPM's forecast is not anchored at pilot_cv but its gain is computed relative to pilot_cv, so about 0.12 of RPM's reported +0.209 'under-prediction of the gain' is the anchor bias, not RPM's slope. In the decision metric, many pilots already have pilot_cv at or below the target. Every method then returns n̂ = n0 and fails by construction, and RPM's anchored curve is non-monotone in about 40% of pilots. The 'structural ill-conditioning' explanation in Section 4.5 is partly an artefact of this anchoring.
issues.evidence: My computation from raw_results.csv and truth_*.npz: mean of pilot_cv_logrmse − truth_logrmse(n0) is −0.187 (n0 = 50), −0.107 (n0 = 100), −0.055 (n0 = 200). It is negative in 78%, 67% and 66% of pilots, and the per-task mean is negative for 34/38 tasks (Diesel:total −1.03, Tecator:fat −0.33). For n0 ≥ 50, mean FLAT |err| is 0.193; after removing the n0-specific mean anchor bias it would be 0.277, against 0.209 for RPM. SLOPE-T: bias −0.146 = anchor bias −0.124 + gain bias −0.022. Gain biases computed with the pilot_cv anchor: RPM +0.209, of which −(−0.124) is the anchor term. Decision metric: pilot_cv ≤ truth(n*) in 31.7% of pilots at n* = 4n0 and 12.8% at 16n0, so failure is guaranteed for every method in those pilots. RPM's forecast at 2n0 exceeds pilot_cv in 39.5% of pilots (RPM-w 41.7%), consistent with the median |log2 err| of exactly 2.0 for RPM, RPM-w, RPM-T and RPM-wT in Table S21. Scripts: /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R4/a1.py, a7.py, a8.py.
issues.corrective_action: (1) Report the anchor bias by n0 and task. (2) Estimate the pilot error without selection optimism, e.g. nested LOGO-CV, or a bias-corrected minimum-CV such as Tibshirani & Tibshirani (2009). Re-run FLAT and SLOPE-T with this anchor and re-evaluate. (3) Make the truth definition consistent with what a practitioner experiences: report results against both log√E[MSE] and the median or geometric-mean RMSE across repetitions. (4) In the gain analysis, compute each method's predicted gain from its own curve (for RPM, fc(n)/fc(n0) with n0 added to the horizon grid), not from pilot_cv. (5) In the decision metric, do not prepend pilot_cv to methods that produce their own curve, and report how many decisions are pre-determined by the anchor. (6) Rewrite the interpretation of FLAT in Section 4.3 and the 'structural' explanation in Section 4.5.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run the pilot stage (same seeds) with (a) nested LOGO-CV or bias-corrected CV error as the anchor and (b) RPM forecasts also at n = n0. Recompute FLAT, SLOPE-T, the gain and decision analyses, and Table 2. If per-repetition test MSEs are stored (re-running the truth stage), also report results against a median-based truth.

issues.title: Leave-one-source-out conformal bands are nominal only when pooled; conditional coverage by pilot size, source and extrapolation ratio fails badly
issues.description: The abstract says 'Bands calibrated across data sets reached nominal coverage'. Recommendation (iii) says that 'for 25–200-sample pilots, honest 80% bands span a factor of about 1.77'. Both rest on coverage pooled over all 10,700 forecast rows (analysis.py T16). Two sources, KSSL and ICRAF, contribute 66% of these rows. The calibration conditions on the extrapolation-ratio bin but not on n0, so the band width is essentially constant across pilot sizes while the forecast error shrinks with n0. The result is systematic under-coverage for small pilots and over-coverage for large ones, and severe under-coverage in the small non-soil sources. Split-conformal guarantees require exchangeability between calibration and test units (sources), which these heterogeneous sources clearly violate, and there are only 8 calibration sources per left-out source.
issues.evidence: Recomputed from raw_results.csv with the authors' algorithm (/tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R4/a5.py). SLOPE-T 80% bands: pooled 79.3% (matches Table S20). By n0: 63.5% (25), 80.7% (50), 91.1% (100), 96.5% (200), with a median width factor of 1.73–1.79 in every n0. By source: CGL 28.8%, Tablets 37.5%, Diesel 49.6%, Tecator 76.1%, ICRAF 87.8%. Ratio bins 128× and 256×: 56.6% and 45.6%. Per-task coverage ranges from 5.8% upward, 8 tasks fall below 60%, and the task-mean coverage is 71.0% (80% nominal) and 88.7% (95% nominal; 7 tasks < 80%). RPM-w 80% bands: n0 = 25 65.2%, n0 = 200 95.3%; Tablets 33.0%, Diesel 54.9%, CGL 56.7%; task-mean 74.3%. Row shares: KSSL 4,160 + ICRAF 2,880 of 10,700 rows.
issues.corrective_action: Calibrate conditionally: Mondrian conformal by n0 × ratio, or normalised conformity scores using a model of the log-error scale as a function of n0, n/n0 and pilot-CV variability. Report coverage at task level and source level, and by n0 and ratio, with clustered CIs. Do not claim nominal coverage or a single 'honest' width factor unless conditional coverage is acceptable. Discuss the exchangeability assumption across sources and the small number of calibration sources. Revise the Abstract and Recommendation (iii).

issues.title: The transferred slope (SLOPE-T, '8.3% per doubling') is in effect a soil-library constant; it fails when transferred across application families, so the general planning recommendation is unsupported
issues.description: SLOPE-T is presented as 'a slope transferred from other calibrations' and recommended for general use (Abstract Significance; Recommendation ii; Conclusions). With leave-one-source-out (LOSO) transfer, the prior for every task is a median dominated by the 23 soil tasks, and it barely varies (−0.099 to −0.084). The evaluation therefore mostly tests whether soil slopes predict soil slopes. When the slope is transferred across application families (fuel, mixtures, meat, fruit, pharma vs soil), SLOPE-T becomes strongly optimistic and clearly worse than both RPM and FLAT. The slope also depends strongly on the n-range over which it is fitted (the curves are concave in log–log). A single 'per doubling' constant is therefore misspecified, and the 8.3% figure reflects each task's grid range as much as its chemistry.
issues.evidence: results/slope_per_doubling.csv: slope_loso_prior ranges only from −0.099 to −0.084. My recomputation (/tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R4/a9.py), keeping the same pilots and anchor and changing only the source of the prior: leave-one-family-out SLOPE-T has mean task error 0.413 and bias −0.28 (vs 0.251 and −0.093 for LOSO). It is worse than RPM on 29/38 tasks (Wilcoxon p < 0.0001) and worse than FLAT on 26/38 (p = 0.0001); transferring soil ↔ non-soil gives 0.413 as well. Range dependence (/tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R4/a6.py) for the 17 tasks with truth up to ≥ 1600: median slope −0.127 over n = 50–100, −0.101 over 50–400 and −0.048 over n ≥ 400, against −0.078 over the full range. SLOPE-T applies one full-range slope at every n0 and horizon.
issues.corrective_action: Evaluate SLOPE-T under leave-one-family-out (or leave-one-domain-out) transfer and report it next to LOSO. State clearly that the 8.3% figure is a soil-dominated median valid over the n-ranges studied. Model the slope as a function of n (or of n and n0) rather than as a constant. Limit Recommendation (ii) and the Significance statement to the domain where the prior was learnt, or validate on external non-soil calibrations.
issues.proposed_experiment: External validation of the transferred-slope rule and of the conformal bands on additional non-soil calibration data sets (e.g. other food, pharmaceutical or process NIR sets with ≥ 1000 samples), with the slope prior and conformal quantiles frozen from the current 38 tasks.

issues.title: The 'noise floor governs the slope' regression is confounded with the n-range of each curve and driven by a few influential tasks
issues.description: Section 4.2 and the Conclusions state that the slope is 'governed mainly by the irreducible-noise fraction' (ρ = +0.59; R² = 0.73). Several problems weaken this. The slope is fitted over each task's own grid (50–100 for CGL and Tecator, up to 6400 for KSSL), and slopes are much steeper at small n (see R4-C01-06). Small data sets also have low noise fractions, so noise fraction and n-range are confounded. The paper's own Table S4 shows that pool size has the strongest correlation with the slope (ρ = +0.62), yet this is not mentioned. The R² is in-sample and post hoc, and it is driven by the four CGL tasks. Finally, the noise fraction and the slope are derived from the same pool and curve, so part of the association is mathematical coupling, since a curve near its asymptote is flat by definition.
issues.evidence: tables/T17_posthoc_slope_explanation.csv: n_pool ρ = 0.624 (p = 2.8e-5) vs noise_frac ρ = 0.590. My recomputation (/tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R4/a6.py): ρ(slope, max n of truth curve) = 0.61; ρ(noise fraction, max n) = 0.56. With slopes on a common range (n = 50–100, all 38 tasks), ρ(noise, slope) = 0.33 (p = 0.045). OLS R² is 0.73 with all tasks, 0.46 (adjusted 0.41) without the 4 CGL tasks and 0.39 without CGL + Tecator, where ρ(noise, slope) = 0.28 (p = 0.13). Leave-one-out CV R² = 0.62.
issues.corrective_action: Compute slopes over a common n-range (or include the n-range as a covariate, or use partial correlations). Report adjusted and cross-validated R², influence diagnostics, and results without CGL and Tecator. Mention n_pool in the text. Rephrase 'governed mainly by' as an exploratory association, and acknowledge the coupling between the noise fraction and the curve's asymptote.

issues.title: Monte-Carlo and test-set error of the ground truth are neither reported nor propagated; the truth is a heavy-tailed arithmetic mean from as few as 8 repetitions
issues.description: The forecasting target is log√(mean test MSE) over 30/16/8 random calibration sets, evaluated on one fixed test split. The stored repetition SEs show non-negligible Monte-Carlo error at several grid points. The repetitions are heavy-tailed (coefficient of variation of the test MSE > 1 in 4 grid points), so the mean is driven by rare failures, and log of the mean exceeds a typical calibration's RMSE (Jensen). The single test split adds further, unquantified error for the small data sets. None of this is reported. Coverage is evaluated as if the truth were exact, which biases coverage downwards for narrow bands (RPM 80% bands have a median half-width of about 0.16 log units). My perturbation analysis shows that the main task-level tests are fairly stable. The issue is reporting and coverage, not reversal of the primary result.
issues.evidence: From truth_*.npz (ridge_se, ridge_mse): MC SE of the truth log RMSE (0.5·SE/MSE) has median 0.014 and maximum 0.126 (Diesel:total, n = 200); 0.093 for KSSL-VisNIR:pH at n = 50 and 0.071 for KSSL-MIR:CEC at n = 3200 (8 reps). The between-repetition CV of the test MSE exceeds 0.5 in 21/189 grid points and 1 in 4. Test sets have 58–60 samples for CGL and Tecator, giving a sampling SD of log RMSE of about 0.09 under Gaussian errors. Perturbation (300 draws; /tmp/claude-0/reviewer_scratch/R4/a3.py, a4.py): with MC noise, SLOPE-T vs RPM p_raw has a 90% range of 0.008–0.023; with a test-set shift, 0.004–0.067 (p < 0.05 in 92% of draws). RPM-w vs RPM stays significant, and FLAT vs RPM is never significant.
issues.corrective_action: Report the MC SE of the truth at each grid point (Table S1 or a new table). Increase repetitions at n ≥ 3200 (8 is too few for heavy-tailed tasks). Store per-repetition test MSE so that median- or geometric-mean truths can be reported. Use repeated group-disjoint test splits (or bootstrap the test set) for the small data sets. Propagate truth uncertainty into the coverage evaluation, e.g. by reporting coverage of the band widened by the truth SE, or by simulation.
issues.proposed_experiment: Re-run the ground-truth stage with ≥ 30 repetitions at every n, per-repetition outputs stored, and 5–10 repeated group-disjoint test splits for Diesel, Tablets, Tecator and CGL. Then recompute Table 2, S8 and the coverage tables.

issues.title: Effect-size estimators, CIs and tests are mismatched and give contradictory signals (Table 2/S8, Table 3/Fig. 9)
issues.description: The paired comparisons report the sample median of the differences with a percentile-bootstrap CI (unreliable for a sample median with n = 38, and unadjusted for multiplicity) next to Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p-values. The Wilcoxon test concerns the pseudo-median (Hodges–Lehmann), not the median. The ablation (Table 3, Fig. 9) pairs mean differences and bootstrap CIs of the mean with Wilcoxon p-values. The result is that the CI and the test disagree in several places, and the text picks whichever signal suits the narrative.
issues.evidence: SLOPE-T vs RPM: Holm p = 0.031, but the median-difference CI [−0.049, +0.0016] includes 0 (statistics.json). PLS FLAT vs RPM: CI [−0.053, −0.006] excludes 0, but Holm p = 0.055. Table 3: type-II ML Δ = +0.063 (CI +0.007 to +0.129, i.e. a 26% higher error than RPM's 0.242), but Wilcoxon Holm p = 1.000 and rank-biserial 0.09. The text calls this a 'small difference' (Section 4.6) while Fig. 9 shows a CI excluding 0. Cut-off 0.5: Δ = +0.033 (variant worse on average), but rank-biserial −0.147 (variant better on the rank majority).
issues.corrective_action: Use one estimand per comparison: either the Hodges–Lehmann estimate with the Wilcoxon-inverted CI (adjusted consistently with Holm, e.g. Bonferroni-level CIs), or mean differences with paired permutation tests and (cluster-)bootstrap CIs. Apply it uniformly in Table 2, S8, Table 3 and Fig. 9. Where mean and rank-based summaries disagree, report both and describe the skew (a few tasks driving the mean).

issues.title: The pre-registered decision endpoint (E5) is reported in an altered form, and its negative result for RPM is not stated in the abstract
issues.description: The pre-registration defines E5 as the error |log2(n̂/n*)|, with failure if the target is never reached. The manuscript replaces this with a dichotomised 'within a factor of two' success rate that does not appear in the pre-registration. It gives no test and no CI, and leaves the failure rates to the supplement. On this registered secondary endpoint, the registered method RPM was among the worst methods (only FLAT, which fails by construction, and EXP3/DF-OLS at 16n0 did worse). The abstract only says that 'no method reliably forecast the sample size'. The post-hoc replacement decision metric (Table S22, balanced accuracy) is uninformative: the outcome prevalence is 97%, and SLOPE-T and FLAT score exactly 0.50 by always answering 'yes' and 'no' respectively. This is not discussed. The anchoring artefact described in R4-C01-04 further undermines the decision analysis.
issues.evidence: Pre-registration 'Decisions (E5)'. Table S21 (tables/T6_sample_size_decisions.csv): within a factor of two, RPM 4.7%/2.0%, IPL3 25.1%/9.2%, SLOPE-T 29.5%/21.1%. The target is never reached by RPM in 51.4% (4n0) and 66.4% (16n0) of pilots, and the median |log2 err| is 2.0/3.6. Table S22 (T14): SLOPE-T sensitivity 1.0, specificity 0.0, balanced accuracy 0.50; prevalence 0.97. EXPERIMENT_LOG.md 14:40: 'Pre-registered decision metric unfavourable to RPM'.
issues.corrective_action: Report the pre-registered metric as specified: per-task mean or median |log2(n̂/n*)|, with non-attainment treated as censored or ranked worst, plus task-level paired tests vs RPM. State in the abstract that RPM performed worse than IPL3 and SLOPE-T on this registered endpoint. Present the factor-of-two rate as a post-hoc dichotomisation. Either drop the balanced-accuracy metric or discuss why a 97%-prevalence outcome makes it uninformative.

issues.title: Simulation and robustness rankings are stated without uncertainty, and some contradict their own numbers
issues.description: The E0 simulation uses a single random population per scenario (6 scenarios, 30 pilots each), and the robustness experiment uses 6 tasks with 10 pilots. Neither reports CIs or tests, yet both are summarised as rankings.
issues.evidence: Section 4.7: 'RPM was the most accurate forecaster (median absolute log error 0.138; RPM-w 0.137)'. RPM-w is lower, and the bootstrap 95% CI of the RPM − RPM-w median difference is [−0.025, +0.029]. 'IPL3 was the most accurate method (0.197 vs 0.221)' at r = 0.5: the CI of the median difference is [−0.061, +0.011] (my bootstrap over 360 rows, which ignores within-pilot clustering and is therefore optimistic). simulation.py uses one population seed per scenario (seed = 17 + i). Section 4.7 cites 'Supplementary Tables S21–S22', which are the decision and gain tables; the simulation is in Tables S26–S27. Table 4 orderings (e.g. 'RPM was less accurate than the no-improvement rule') rest on 6 tasks with no test; the minimum attainable two-sided Wilcoxon p with n = 6 is 0.031.
issues.corrective_action: Simulate several independent populations per scenario and report MC SEs or CIs for every simulated median. Correct the 'most accurate' wording and the table cross-reference. For Table 4, give per-task values or CIs, and describe the orderings as descriptive.
issues.proposed_experiment: Repeat E0 with ≥ 20 independently drawn populations (covariance seed and β) per scenario and report MC CIs.

issues.title: Row-pooled summaries, uncorrected exploratory correlations and imprecise p-value reporting
issues.description: Several secondary summaries are pooled over forecast rows. Tasks then contribute 60 to 520 rows each, so the large soil libraries dominate. Table 2's caption says errors are averaged within each task, but the 'Within ±20%' column, coverage (42.3%/58.3%) and decision percentages are row-pooled. '117,700 forecasts' counts 11 methods × 10,700 rows and overstates the information content relative to the 38 tasks and 9 sources. Section 4.9 reports five uncorrected Spearman tests with 'p = 0.000' and raw code variable names (eigen_decay_exponent, theory_fit_err, noise_frac, n_pool).
issues.evidence: analysis.py summary_table (pct_within_20 over rows), coverage_table (coverage_rows), decision_table (pct_within_factor2 over rows). Rows per task: CGL and Tecator 60, KSSL 520; KSSL + ICRAF = 7,040/10,700 rows (66%). tables/T13b_error_correlates.csv: p = 1.6e-4 and 2.4e-4 are printed as 'p = 0.000' in Section 4.9.
issues.corrective_action: Report task-level (equally weighted) versions of all secondary percentages, or state the weighting explicitly. Report exact p-values (e.g. p = 0.0002). Correct or flag exploratory correlation families. Replace code variable names with descriptive labels. Present the number of independent units (tasks, sources) next to forecast counts.

issues.title: The κ-collapse 'direct test' uses a strawman reference
issues.description: Section 4.1 presents the collapse statistic (0.041 vs 0.519) as a direct test of the structural assumption. The collapse statistic is computed only on penalties with df2/n < 0.8 and after the theory prefactor is applied. The reference is the across-n SD of raw log test MSE over all 53 penalties, including the near-interpolation region, with no prefactor. The reference therefore mostly measures how much the learning curve drops with n (plus the blow-up at small penalties). It is not a plausible alternative hypothesis, so the contrast does not test the κ-mapping specifically.
issues.evidence: analysis.py collapse_dispersion: ref = mean(std(log ridge_mu_mse[:len(pts)], axis=0)) over all μ, with no validity mask and no rescaling; theory_validity applies ok = d2/n < 0.8 and the prefactor (1 − df2/n)/(1 + 1/n) only to the collapse curves. Table S3; Section 4.1.
issues.corrective_action: Compare the κ-collapse with non-trivial alternatives restricted to the same validity region: prefactor-rescaled errors against μ, against μ·n, or against an empirically optimal 1-D reparametrisation. Report the per-task distribution with uncertainty.

recommendation_rationale: The confirmatory pre-registered result (RPM is markedly less optimistic and more accurate than IPL3 and the other curve-shape extrapolations) is statistically sound and survives every re-analysis I ran, including clustering by data source. The paper's practical message, however, rests mainly on post-hoc and exploratory analyses. Those analyses use the pilot-CV anchor (RPM-w, SLOPE-T, FLAT parity, the 8.3% slope, calibrated bands, the decision and gain metrics), and their inference is weaker than presented. Specifically: the significance claims for SLOPE-T and RPM-w do not survive the paper's own PLS and ICRAF-exclusion sensitivity analyses, and the text misstates both. Equivalence is asserted without an equivalence test. The pilot-CV anchor carries an optimistic bias that makes FLAT look competitive through cancelling errors. The conformal bands are nominal only when pooled. The transferred slope fails when transferred across application families. None of this requires new data, and most of it can be fixed by re-analysis of the released per-pilot outputs. Re-running the pilot stage with a bias-corrected anchor and increasing ground-truth repetitions is computationally modest. Abstract, Significance, Recommendations (ii)–(iii) and Conclusions must be revised accordingly.
